---
title: 'Exercise 2: Colour that supports comparison'
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, comment=NA, message=FALSE,
                      warning=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5)
```

Complete Tasks 1-2 in class (about 12 minutes). Run the examples, replace each `---` in the code, and run your completed chunks. Keep one palette choice and one distribution plot. The sections marked optional provide further practice; you are welcome to continue through the rest of the document.

If patchwork is not installed, run the installation chunk below once. Skip it if you installed patchwork in Exercise 1. `eval = FALSE` means it is skipped when knitting, but you can run it interactively.

```{r install-patchwork, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("patchwork")
```

Run the library chunk each time you start a new R session, then the data chunk. The data chunk removes rows missing variables we need and gives the smoking-status groups readable names. Each row is one participant.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
```

```{r load-data}
d_blomkvist <- read_csv("data/blomkvist.csv")
d_blomkvist <- drop_na(d_blomkvist, smoker, age, rt_hand_d, rt_hand_nd)
# Change group names in the data, so later plots use readable labels.
d_blomkvist <- mutate(d_blomkvist,
                     smoker = factor(smoker, levels = c("former", "no", "yes"),
                                     labels = c("Former smoker", "Never smoked",
                                                "Current smoker")))
```

Now run the plot chunk. It maps smoking status to point colour; the reaction times are in milliseconds. Assignment stores the plot without displaying it; run `plot_rt` to display it.

```{r base-plot}
# <- stores the plot in an object (a variable) called plot_rt.
plot_rt <- ggplot(d_blomkvist,
                  aes(x = rt_hand_d, y = rt_hand_nd, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point()
```

## Task 1: Choose a palette for comparing groups

`plot_rt` now contains the plot. We can display it by running `plot_rt`, or reuse it with `plot_rt + ...`. Below, `<-` stores each new version under a different name (`plot_palette_a` and `plot_palette_b`), leaving the original `plot_rt` unchanged.

**Question:** Which palette makes the smoking-status groups easier to distinguish?

Run this chunk unchanged. A colour scale changes the colours used for the existing mapping; it does not change the data or point positions. `scale_colour_discrete()` uses the default categorical palette. `scale_colour_viridis_d()` supplies another categorical palette (`d` means discrete). Smoking status is categorical, so a continuous colour scale would not be appropriate here. The patchwork operator `|` puts the plots next to each other.

```{r palette-choice, fig.width=11}
plot_palette_a <- plot_rt +
  scale_colour_discrete()
plot_palette_b <- plot_rt +
  scale_colour_viridis_d()
# patchwork places the plots side by side for comparison.
plot_palette_a | plot_palette_b
```

Which palette would you choose: A (left, default) or B (right, viridis)? Consider how easily readers can distinguish the groups and where the figure will be viewed.

Write your choice and reason here: ___

Replace `---` below with `scale_colour_discrete` or `scale_colour_viridis_d` to apply your chosen palette. Keep the parentheses: you are adding a scale function to a ggplot. Run your completed chunk.

```{r chosen-palette}
my_palette_plot <- plot_rt + ---()
my_palette_plot
```

## Task 2: Keep overlapping distributions visible

**Question:** How do age distributions differ between smoking-status groups?

First complete the mappings below. `fill` colours the inside of each density curve; `colour` colours its outline. Replace both `---` blanks with the column identifying smoking-status groups, so the interiors and outlines describe the same groups. Age is numeric, and smoking status is categorical.

Each scale controls one aesthetic: `scale_fill_viridis_d()` does not change the outlines, and `scale_colour_viridis_d()` does not change the interiors. Using matching palettes keeps the two aesthetics consistent.

```{r distribution-mapping}
plot_age <- ggplot(d_blomkvist,
                   aes(x = age, fill = ---, colour = ---)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() + scale_colour_viridis_d()
```

Now run the comparison below. `alpha` controls opacity: 0 is fully transparent and 1 is fully opaque. `position = "identity"` overlays the curves rather than stacking them. Keep the data and palette fixed so that you can judge only the effect of transparency.

```{r distribution-choice, fig.width=11}
plot_opaque <- plot_age +
  geom_density(alpha = 1, position = "identity")
plot_transparent <- plot_age +
  geom_density(alpha = .25, position = "identity")
plot_opaque | plot_transparent
```

Which version would you choose: A (left, opaque) or B (right, transparent)? Explain which features of the distributions are easier to compare.

Write your choice and reason here: ___

Replace `---` in the next chunk with a number between 0 and 1, then try a second value. Choose the version that makes the group distributions easiest to compare; you do not have to use either example value.

```{r chosen-opacity}
my_opacity <- ---
my_distribution <- plot_age +
  geom_density(alpha = my_opacity, position = "identity")
my_distribution
```

Finally, run the count below. Each density curve has total area 1, regardless of the group size: a taller peak is not evidence that a group has more participants. Use the counts to identify information the density plot does not communicate.

```{r group-sizes}
count(d_blomkvist, smoker)
```

After checking the group sizes, what does your chosen figure still hide?

Write your answer here: ___

## Optional: Compare a continuous scale and its reversal

Here the question changes: how does age vary across the reaction-time plot? Age is numeric, so map it to a continuous colour scale rather than the discrete scale used for smoking status. Run the first chunk unchanged. Notice that the legend is now a colour bar: by default, younger ages are dark and older ages are bright.

```{r continuous-age-colour}
plot_age_colour <- ggplot(d_blomkvist,
                         aes(x = rt_hand_d, y = rt_hand_nd,
                             colour = age)) +
  geom_point()
plot_age_default <- plot_age_colour + scale_colour_viridis_c()
plot_age_default
```

Now reverse the palette so that darker means older. Replace `---` below with `-1`, run the chunk, and compare the colour bars. The default direction is `1`; reversing it changes the colours, not the data or point positions. Which direction better matches how you expect readers to interpret age?

```{r reverse-age-colour, fig.width=11}
plot_age_reversed <- plot_age_colour +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(direction = ---)
plot_age_default | plot_age_reversed
```

Check which end of each colour bar represents older participants.

## Optional: Set colours manually

The names in `my_colours` match the group names in the data. The hex codes specify their colours. Edit one code and run this chunk to store your palette.

```{r define-manual-palette}
# Named values keep colours stable if the order of groups changes.
my_colours <- c("Former smoker" = "#0072B2",
                "Never smoked" = "#D55E00",
                "Current smoker" = "#009E73")
```

Run the next chunk to preview your colours as swatches. Check that the three groups are easy to distinguish before applying the palette to the plot.

```{r preview-manual-palette}
scales::show_col(my_colours)
```

Now replace `---` with the name of the object containing your colours and run the plot chunk. If you edit the palette again, rerun the definition, preview, and plot chunks in order.

```{r manual-palette}
plot_rt + scale_colour_manual(values = ---)
```

Try one colour change. Does it improve the comparison? Explain why.

Write your answer here: ___

## Optional: Compare outline-only densities

This version uses `colour` without `fill`, leaving the interiors empty. Run it and compare it with your transparent version. Consider whether removing fill helps readers follow the curves or makes the groups harder to identify.

```{r outline-density}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = .8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d()
```

Compare this with `my_distribution`. Which would you use, and why?
